summary: Leo Pekelis (Chief Scientist, Gradient) describes how Gradient trained Albatross, a finance-expert LLM, framed by two broader observations: foundational models are proliferating across companies and context lengths have grown roughly 40x in the past year (from ~100k tokens). These observations support Gradient's thesis that LLMs are not one-size-fits-all and that generalist base models fall short for specialized domains. Gradient operates as an AI Foundry offering custom language models plus workflow primitives. For finance specifically, two components matter: a domain-specific finance language model and extended context length. For the finance LLM, Leo explains that general-purpose models are broad but shallow on technical financial data; even a 176B-parameter model needs thousands of relevant documents in pre-training to exceed 50% accuracy. Because financial data is too voluminous to review manually, Gradient built an automated data pipeline using membership-inference-style techniques to detect whether a document was likely already in the base model's training data, filtering down to a manageable set for human review, then applying synthetic data augmentation for upsampling and format variation. The training recipe has two stages: continual pre-training (next-token prediction on a base model like Llama) and alignment via supervised fine-tuning plus preference optimization. Leo then pivots to hallucinations, attributing causes to outdated training data and source-reference divergence from automated collection bugs. At Gradient, in-context learning is considered the most direct and sample-efficient hallucination mitigation. The bottleneck is context length: few-shot examples exhaust prompt space, complex preprocessing becomes brittle, and RAG struggles with interrelated chunks. Extending context to ~1M tokens allows thousands of in-prompt examples at inference time and leverages native transformer attention for complex implicit reasoning, demonstrated with a Mark Twain style-generation example whose output convinced a separate critic model of authenticity down to theme, characters, and setting. The punchline: long-context models yield more grounded, robust systems with fewer moving parts, reducing hallucinations. Gradient emphasizes transparent, verifiable benchmarks and open-sources both solutions on Hugging Face: the v-alpha-tross finance model (Llama 2 based), competitive on general Open LLM benchmarks and better on finance-specific tasks versus peers, and a 1M-context Llama 3 model achieving 100% needle-in-a-haystack above 1M tokens with substantial improvements on NVIDIA's Ruler long-context benchmark, placing it alongside flagship long-context models like Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, and Command R Plus. Leo closes by noting these are just two pieces of a larger puzzle in building an AI financial expert.

sections.title: Introduction and LLM Landscape Observations
sections.summary: Leo introduces himself and Gradient, noting exponential growth in foundational models and ~40x growth in context length over the past year, motivating the thesis that LLMs are not one-size-fits-all.

sections.title: AI Foundry and Finance Solutions
sections.summary: Gradient's AI Foundry combines custom language models with workflow primitives. For finance, two components are key: a domain-specific finance LLM and extended context length.

sections.title: Why a Domain-Specific Finance LLM
sections.summary: General-purpose models are broad but shallow on technical financial data. Even a 176B model needs thousands of relevant pre-training documents to exceed 50% accuracy, motivating domain-specific training.

sections.title: Automated Data Pipeline
sections.summary: Financial data is too voluminous for manual review. Gradient built an automated pipeline using membership-inference-style techniques to detect if documents were already in the base model's training data, filtering down for human review, then synthetic data augmentation for upsampling and format variation.

sections.title: Training Pipeline
sections.summary: The recipe has two stages: continual pre-training (next-token prediction on a base model like Llama) and alignment via supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, analogized to reading textbooks versus taking an exam.

sections.title: Hallucinations and In-Context Learning
sections.summary: Hallucinations stem from outdated training data and source-reference divergence. In-context learning is Gradient's preferred, most sample-efficient mitigation, but is bottlenecked by context length—limiting few-shot examples, complicating preprocessing, and degrading RAG on interrelated chunks.

sections.title: Extended Context Capabilities
sections.summary: ~1M-token contexts enable thousands of in-prompt examples at inference time and leverage native transformer attention for complex implicit reasoning. A Mark Twain style-generation demo produced stories convincing a separate critic model of authenticity down to theme, characters, and setting. Long-context models yield more grounded, robust systems with fewer moving parts, reducing hallucinations.

sections.title: Open-Source Models and Benchmarks
sections.summary: Gradient emphasizes transparent, verifiable benchmarks and open-sources both solutions on Hugging Face: the v-alpha-tross finance model (Llama 2 based), competitive on general Open LLM benchmarks and better on finance-specific tasks versus peers, and a 1M-context Llama 3 model achieving 100% needle-in-a-haystack above 1M tokens with substantial Ruler (NVIDIA) improvements, placing it alongside flagship models like Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, and Command R Plus. Leo closes noting these are two pieces of a larger puzzle.

demonstrations: Scrubbed Mark Twain books of identifying information, fed them into a long-context model's prompt, and asked it to generate new stories in the same style; a separate critic model judged outputs as plausibly authored by Twain down to theme, characters, and setting.
Released v-alpha-tross (finance-tuned Llama 2) and a 1M-context Llama 3 model on Hugging Face with public benchmark results.
limitations: Generalist models are broad not deep on technical financial information.
Financial data is too voluminous to review manually, necessitating automated pipelines.
In-context learning is bottlenecked by context length.
Few-shot prompting exhausts prompt space before examples are exhausted.
Complex preprocessing pipelines for long inputs are brittle and error-prone.
RAG performs poorly when chunks must reference other chunks.
The two presented solutions are only two pieces of a larger puzzle in building an AI financial expert.
